## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Kāsāvajātaka* (Ja 221), translated as *The Ocher Robe*, is a story in the Jātaka collection of the Pali canon. The narrative opening records that the Buddha related this story while residing at Jetavana, occasioned by Devadatta [Fausböll 1879]. In the story of the past, the Bodhisatta was born as the leader of an elephant herd (*yūthapati*) [Sahni 2008; Fausböll 1879]. A hunter—identified in the *samodhāna* with Devadatta—disguised himself in the yellow ascetic robes (*kāsāva*) of a renunciant in order to approach, deceive, and kill elephants for their ivory [Sahni 2008; Fausböll 1879]. Realizing the hunter's deceit and that he was unworthy of the sacred robe, the Bodhisatta spared his life out of reverence for the garment but drove him from the forest under warning never to return [Sahni 2008; Fausböll 1879]. Pragati Sahni highlights the tale as an ethically significant narrative in which animals act as conscious moral agents [Sahni 2008].
